objects.title: MAAT
objects.summary: A riverfront museum where contemporary architecture, art and the Tagus meet.
objects.why: It works as a strong entry point into Belém because the building, the riverfront and nearby cultural places can be explored as one connected experience.

objects.title: Belém
objects.summary: A riverfront district combining monuments, museums, gardens, food and public space.
objects.why: Belém is better experienced as a connected cluster than as a checklist of separate attractions.

objects.title: Lisbon through architecture
objects.summary: A self-guided architectural thread linking buildings, streets and public spaces across the city.
objects.why: It demonstrates how LBNB can create an experience by connecting several Places and Stories without requiring a formal tour.

objects.title: The Tagus riverfront
objects.summary: A story about how Lisbon meets the Tagus through infrastructure, monuments and contemporary public space.
objects.why: The river is not just scenery; it is one of the systems that explains the city.

objects.title: Alfama
objects.summary: A hillside neighbourhood of narrow streets, stairs, viewpoints and everyday life.
objects.why: Alfama proves that a neighbourhood itself can be the discovery, without needing a single landmark to justify it.

objects.title: Fado and the city
objects.summary: A cultural thread connecting voice, neighbourhood, memory and performance spaces.
objects.why: The Story layer can explain why an experience matters instead of reducing fado to a venue category.

objects.title: A viewpoint above Alfama
objects.summary: A pause above the neighbourhood that reveals its topography and relationship to the river.
objects.why: A viewpoint becomes useful when it is connected back to the neighbourhood beneath it.

objects.title: Neighbourhood food in Alfama
objects.summary: A food stop understood as part of the neighbourhood rather than an isolated restaurant search.
objects.why: It connects eating to the streets, culture and rhythm of Alfama.

objects.title: Calçada portuguesa
objects.summary: Lisbon’s black-and-white stone paving turns the ground itself into public design.
objects.why: It is a perfect Story-first object: a familiar surface becomes meaningful once you understand its craft, pattern and identity.

objects.title: Rossio / Baixa
objects.summary: A central part of Lisbon where paving, squares, streets and reconstructed urban order overlap.
objects.why: The Place gives physical context to the Story of calçada portuguesa.

objects.title: Pattern in Lisbon’s public space
objects.summary: A visual story about how paving, geometry and repeated materials shape the experience of the street.
objects.why: It expands a detail into a way of seeing the city.

objects.title: Make / Taste Lisbon
objects.summary: A hands-on food experience centred on making, tasting and understanding a local recipe.
objects.why: The subject can change—pastry, bread, bacalhau—but the product logic stays the same: doing becomes a route into place and culture.

objects.title: The workshop kitchen
objects.summary: The actual place where the hands-on food experience happens.
objects.why: Separating Place from Experience lets the same location host different activities over time.

objects.title: The pastry tradition
objects.summary: The cultural and culinary context behind a familiar Portuguese pastry.
objects.why: It turns tasting into understanding, without making the Story a lecture.

objects.title: Oriente / contemporary Lisbon
objects.summary: A contemporary transport and urban district that breaks with the postcard image of Lisbon.
objects.why: It proves that the product can reveal modern Lisbon as strongly as historic Lisbon.

objects.title: Modern Lisbon
objects.summary: A story about the city’s contemporary architecture, infrastructure and newer urban districts.
objects.why: It prevents Lisbon from being frozen into a historic-tourism image.

objects.title: A contemporary Lisbon thread
objects.summary: A route connecting modern buildings, infrastructure and public spaces.
objects.why: A Journey can be assembled around a way of seeing, not only around attractions.

objects.title: Beirut
objects.summary: A city best entered through neighbourhoods, streets, architecture, food and the relationships between them.
objects.why: Beirut should never be flattened into a short list of attractions; the graph is particularly useful here because identities overlap constantly.

objects.title: Beirut through architecture
objects.summary: A way to read Beirut through apartment buildings, façades, streets and surviving fragments from different periods.
objects.why: Architecture becomes a lens into the city instead of a specialist category isolated from everyday life.

objects.title: The Lebanese table
objects.summary: Food understood as a network of dishes, rituals, ingredients, regions and people.
objects.why: It connects what you eat to culture and place instead of reducing food discovery to restaurant rankings.

objects.title: A Beirut neighbourhood
objects.summary: A neighbourhood-level entry into the city, where everyday movement becomes part of discovery.
objects.why: The product can move from city to neighbourhood without changing object systems.

objects.title: Mar Mikhael
objects.summary: A Beirut neighbourhood shaped by older buildings, workshops, cafés, nightlife and ongoing urban change.
objects.why: It is dense enough to connect architecture, food, craft and social life in one graph.

objects.title: A venue in Mar Mikhael
objects.summary: A specific café, workshop, gallery or venue can sit inside the larger neighbourhood object.
objects.why: This demonstrates the Place-within-Place hierarchy we designed.

objects.title: A Beirut food walk
objects.summary: A flexible food thread through bakeries, cafés and neighbourhood stops.
objects.why: It connects several Places while the Story layer explains what each stop means.

objects.title: Beyond Mar Mikhael
objects.summary: The next neighbourhood becomes a continuation rather than a separate search result.
objects.why: Discovery should keep flowing spatially through the city.

objects.title: Jbeil / Byblos
objects.summary: A historic Mediterranean town where archaeology, old streets, the harbour and present-day life overlap.
objects.why: It can connect heritage to contemporary experience in one compact destination graph.

objects.title: Old town / harbour
objects.summary: The lived urban and coastal fabric around the archaeological layers of Jbeil.
objects.why: The historic site becomes more meaningful when connected to the town around it.

objects.title: Layers of Byblos
objects.summary: A Story connecting ancient settlement, archaeology, the old town and the contemporary coast.
objects.why: History is presented as a layer within a living place, not as a detached timeline.

objects.title: Food on the coast
objects.summary: A food stop that belongs to the coastal experience rather than a standalone restaurant ranking.
objects.why: It connects place, sea and eating into the same Journey.

objects.title: From coast to the Beqaa
objects.summary: A larger Journey thread connecting Jbeil / Byblos, inland landscapes and Baalbek.
objects.why: It demonstrates how individual discoveries can become a wider route across Lebanon.

objects.title: Baalbek
objects.summary: A monumental archaeological place in the Beqaa centred on extraordinary Roman temple remains.
objects.why: The Place can open into history, landscape and a wider Lebanon Journey instead of ending at the monument itself.

objects.title: The temple complex
objects.summary: A Story about the scale, layers and meaning of the temple complex at Baalbek.
objects.why: It provides depth only when the user wants it, while the reel remains primarily visual.

objects.title: The Beqaa
objects.summary: The wider inland landscape surrounding Baalbek and connecting the site to a larger region.
objects.why: It stops a major monument from becoming an isolated pin on a map.

objects.title: Beirut food walk
objects.summary: A food experience that can connect bakeries, kitchens and neighbourhood stories.
objects.why: The experience becomes richer because it is connected to the Lebanese Table Story.

objects.title: A bakery / kitchen
objects.summary: A real food-making place that can anchor a Story or Experience.
objects.why: The platform can connect the people and places behind food, not only finished dishes.

objects.title: Regional food traditions
objects.summary: A Story connecting dishes and ingredients to different regions, seasons and communities.
objects.why: It expands one table into a broader cultural map of Lebanon.

objects.title: Lebanon
objects.summary: A country of closely connected coasts, cities, mountains, valleys and villages.
objects.why: The archive becomes more useful when each stay opens into the place around it.

objects.title: Batroun & North
objects.summary: A coastal and mountain territory extending from Batroun into villages, valleys and highland landscapes.
objects.why: Stays here can connect the coast to inland villages, food, craft and mountain routes.

objects.title: Bsharri & the Cedars
objects.summary: High mountain landscapes, cedar country and villages around the Qadisha Valley.
objects.why: Accommodation becomes an entry point into landscape, heritage, walking and local culture.

objects.title: Ehden
objects.summary: A mountain town and summer destination in North Lebanon.
objects.why: Ehden links mountain stays with food, landscape and regional stories.

objects.title: The Chouf
objects.summary: Mountain towns, historic villages and landscapes south-east of Beirut.
objects.why: The Chouf is best understood through connected villages, houses, food and cultural landscapes.

objects.title: Kesrouan
objects.summary: A varied mountain-and-coast district north of Beirut.
objects.why: Stays here open into villages, ski country, historic houses and the coast.

objects.title: Metn
objects.summary: A broad territory of Beirut’s eastern hills, towns and mountain edges.
objects.why: The area connects everyday residential places to mountain towns and local routes.

objects.title: Aley
objects.summary: Mountain towns and villages above Beirut, long connected to summer life and movement across Mount Lebanon.
objects.why: Aley is a useful bridge between city, mountain and village experiences.

objects.title: South Lebanon
objects.summary: Southern towns, landscapes and routes extending beyond Beirut and Mount Lebanon.
objects.why: These stays expand the graph beyond the familiar north-and-Beirut circuit.

objects.title: Mount Lebanon
objects.summary: A wide band of hills, towns and villages surrounding Beirut and extending inland.
objects.why: It connects residential stays to mountain landscapes and village life.

reels.caption: The building is only the beginning. Follow the riverfront from here.
You don’t have to find a monument to discover Lisbon. Sometimes the street is enough.
Look down. Part of Lisbon’s identity is already under your feet.
Some places are better understood by making something, not just looking at it.
Lisbon didn’t stop being built when the postcards were printed.
Beirut is not one story. Start with one street and follow what connects to it.
One Beirut neighbourhood can contain architecture, food, craft and nightlife at once.
History is more interesting when the town around it is still alive.
The monument is extraordinary. The interesting part is what it connects to beyond itself.
A Lebanese table is not one dish. It is a network of people, places and rituals.
A stay can be the beginning of a neighbourhood. Start on a Beirut rooftop, then follow what surrounds it.
Stay in the mountains, then let the place around you become the discovery.
A mountain stay can open into landscape, heritage and the wider Bsharri region.
In Deir El Qamar, the stay and the historic town should be understood together.
A village stay becomes a doorway into inland Jbeil and the coast beyond it.
The Lebanon graph should not stop at Beirut and the north. Continue south.
